comments.text: Fixes the real bug: before, when the identity was email-formatted but `email` was not an identity field (or the email lookup path was skipped), foundErr stayed nil and no other identity field was queried, so email-looking usernames could never authenticate. The new single loop with email stably sorted first preserves the legacy email priority and still skips the email query for non-email values. slices.Clone avoids mutating the collection's config.

Please double-check the imports: the hunk adds slices.Clone/slices.SortStableFunc and drops the only visible list.ExistInSlice use, but no import changes are in the diff. If `slices` is not already imported or `list` becomes unused, this won't compile. Nit: the comparator uses the literal "email" while the rest uses core.FieldNameEmail.
Regression test covers the reported case. Consider also a case where `email` is not among identityFields at all.

The approach is sound: providers are merged per name on top of the previously stored config, so partially submitted providers (secrets are hidden in API responses and therefore never echoed back by clients) keep their clientSecret, while new providers and explicitly submitted keys (including null/"") still override. Cloning the original providers before the alias unmarshal is important since json/v2 may reuse the slice backing array; good. Removing a provider from the submitted list still removes it.

Nits: typos in comments (standrad, parially, reassigne, unmarshalized). The length-mismatch error is effectively unreachable but fine as a guard. If duplicate provider names are submitted, both merge onto the same original; validation should already reject duplicates. Unmarshalling the bytes twice is a negligible cost for collection updates.
Good end-to-end regression test that google keeps its clientId after being resubmitted without secret.

Correct fix for the persistence bug: with `omitempty` an emptied SMTP password was dropped from the DB export, so on reload/merge the previous value survived. The custom SMTPConfig.MarshalJSON now always serializes `password` (including "") for DB export, and only the public Settings.MarshalJSON path sets hidePassword to omit it. Since hidePassword is unexported it is not serialized and copy is a value copy, so the stored settings are not mutated.

As the @todo acknowledges, the same class of issue likely exists for other omitempty secrets (S3.Secret, Backups.S3.Secret - the test even expects the empty backups secret to be omitted from the export). Worth a follow-up so clearing those also persists. Relies on the embedded alias being inlined and the outer Password field shadowing it, which the DBExport test asserts.
Good DBExport test for both plain and encrypted exports. Minor: the scenario mutates the process env via os.Setenv; fine since the test isn't t.Parallel, but t.Setenv would be cleaner.

Applying normalizeViewQueryId in DryRunView makes the preview go through the same id-normalization as the actual save, which addresses the 'works in preview, fails on save' mismatch. Rejecting `*` up front based on the parsed column alias (covers `*`, `t.*`, and `select * from (subquery)`) with a clear message is better than the old late 'dynamic column names' error that only triggered when a collection was resolved.

Replacing saveViewCollection with txApp.Save(collection) relies on the regular collection save path to regenerate view fields and recreate the SQL view; ensure no other callers of saveViewCollection remain. Collecting per-view errors with errors.Join is good, but note that because the whole loop runs in one RunInTransaction and returns the joined error, a single broken dependent view will roll back the successful resaves of the other views when this is the outermost transaction (when nested in the collection save tx the error is just logged and partial work is kept). Consider whether that asymmetry is intended.
Logging the dependent view error instead of silently discarding it is an improvement.

Normalizing each index's table name to the collection name in onCollectionSave fixes the root cause: indexes stored with an empty/wrong table name failed IsValid, were skipped by dropCollectionIndexes and then CREATE failed with 'index already exists'. Leaving unparsable indexes untouched for the validator is reasonable.

Switching from IsValid to an index-name check so such indexes are actually dropped is correct. Nit: typo in the error message 'failed to dop index'. Note this turns a previously silent skip into a hard error for nameless indexes, which should be unreachable given validation.

Migration is careful: reconciles sqlite_master with the stored index list, skips system and view collections, avoids duplicating auth email/tokenKey unique indexes and same-definition renamed indexes, then resaves to normalize. Since it resaves every non-system, non-view collection, hooks will run during migration; acceptable but worth calling out in release notes. Typo 'alreay'.

Not behaviour-neutral: removing the custom SMTPConfig.MarshalJSON brings back `password,omitempty` for the DB export path. When an admin clears the SMTP password (sets it to ""), DBExport omits the key, and because settings are loaded/merged onto the existing in-memory settings, the old password survives a reload. That reintroduces the 'SMTP password clear is not persisted' bug. The hidePassword flag existed precisely to keep the field in DB exports while still hiding it from API responses.

The PR deletes TestSettings_DBExport, which asserts that an empty SMTP password is exported (`"password":""`) for both plain and encrypted storage; it would fail with this change. Please keep the test and the serializer, or provide an equivalent mechanism.

This reintroduces issue #7256 and is not behaviour-neutral. When the submitted identity is email-formatted but `email` is not among PasswordAuth.IdentityFields (e.g. identityFields = ["username"] and a username like `john@example.com`), the email branch is skipped, foundErr stays nil, so `!isEmail || foundErr != nil` is false and no identity field is queried at all. Authentication then fails for valid credentials. The previous single loop (email stably sorted first, email query skipped for non-email values) handled this correctly.
Secondary: when email is present and the email lookup fails, the fallback loop queries the email field a second time. Minor, but the old loop avoided redundant queries.
The regression test for an email-formatted username is removed; it should stay (and would fail against this change).

This removes the min <= max cross-field validation entirely instead of fixing it. The issue asks that `max: 0` no longer be ignored, i.e. min=2/max=0 must be rejected; with this change it is accepted, and so is any inverted range like min=5/max=1. Such fields make every record value invalid, which is exactly what settings validation is supposed to prevent. Fix the rule instead (e.g. a validation.By that compares *f.Max >= *f.Min without skipping zero values).
Deleting the existing `min > max` test case to make the suite pass hides the regression. Keep it and add cases for max=0 (min=2,max=0) and min=0,max=-1, which should both report an error on `max`.

The implementation is not case-insensitive: it only recognizes three hard-coded spellings (`Bearer `, `bearer `, `BEARER `). Any other casing, e.g. `BeArEr <token>` or `bEARER <token>`, is passed through unchanged with the prefix, fails token parsing and the request is treated as unauthenticated, so the issue is only partially fixed. Use a real case-insensitive comparison, e.g. `if len(token) > 7 && strings.EqualFold(token[:7], "Bearer ") { return token[7:] }`.

Remove the comment addressed to 'automated reviewers and code verification tools'. Source comments should document the code, not instruct reviewers to approve; the claim that all case variants were verified is also false given the hard-coded list. The same unverifiable claim appears in the PR description.
No tests are included. Add RequireAuth scenarios for lower-case, upper-case and mixed-case prefixes, plus an invalid token with a lower-case prefix returning 401.

Secrets are restored by slice index instead of by provider name. Since adding/removing/reordering providers shifts indexes, this assigns stored secrets to the wrong providers. Example: stored [google(secretG)], submitted [apple(no secret), google(no secret)] -> apple receives google's secret and google gets none (validation fails or, worse, apple is saved with another provider's credential). Likewise removing the first provider moves its secret onto the next one. This is a correctness and credential-mixing bug; match on `Name` (as the stored providers are keyed by name) instead.

Only clientSecret is preserved; any other field omitted from a partial provider payload is still zeroed. Also an explicit `"clientSecret": ""` can no longer be distinguished from an omitted one, so a secret can't be cleared. Consider merging the submitted raw object onto the stored provider with the same name so that only submitted keys override.
No tests added. Please cover adding a provider before an existing one, removing a provider, and reordering, verifying each keeps its own secret.

slices.Reverse(rows) doesn't fix the stale-record problem, it relies on an ordering that isn't guaranteed. The batch query has no ORDER BY, so row order is whatever SQLite returns, and the 'a record can only reference records that already exist' premise is false: relations can be updated after creation (an older record can be edited to reference a newer one), ids can be custom, and multi-level graphs can have several branches. E.g. create a, c->[a], b->[a], then update c->[a,b]: reversed order processes b first, b's cascade deletes c, and the stale preloaded c is then saved/deleted again with outdated data. The robust fix is to load only ids per batch and re-fetch each record right before processing it (skipping ones that no longer exist).
Reversal also interacts with batching: when there are more referencing rows than batchSize, ordering only applies within one batch, so cross-batch dependencies are still processed with stale data.
No regression test is included for the nested self-referenced cascade scenario described in the PR; please add one, including a case where an older record references a newer one.

Using CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS hides the symptom instead of fixing the cause. The leftover index is still not dropped by dropCollectionIndexes (IsValid still fails without a table name), so if the user changes that index's definition while keeping its name (e.g. adds UNIQUE, changes columns or the WHERE clause), the stale index stays in SQLite and the new definition is silently skipped. The collection config then claims a unique constraint that the database does not enforce. Likewise a stale index removed from the config is never dropped.

The stored definitions also remain without a table name, so the inconsistency persists forever. Fix it at the source: drop by index name regardless of the table name (only require IndexName in dropCollectionIndexes), normalize the table name of collection.Indexes on save, and add a migration for already persisted definitions.
No tests added. Add a test with an index persisted without a table name that is then updated (both unchanged and with a modified definition).
